strengths: Clearly identifies and motivates a real problem in domain representation learning for policy adaptation: the entanglement of static domain factors with transient dynamical variations when using temporally-local context for dynamics prediction.

The proposed 'Lagged Context Dynamical Prediction' is simple, intuitive, and well-illustrated via a clean analytical toy example (Appendix A) that clarifies why increasing the context offset filters out instantaneous variation.

Extensive empirical validation: linear-probe accuracy and reconstruction loss (Table 2) plus t-SNE visualizations (Figs. 3, 6) consistently show improved representation quality as Δt increases, approaching supervised-representation quality.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contributions of representation quality (Δt) versus representation utilization (conditioning vs. prior-biasing vs. joint prediction target), which helps attribute performance gains to specific design choices (Table 4).
Additional robustness checks are included, e.g., sensitivity to guidance scale (Appendix C.1) and to context source at deployment time (Appendix C.2), supporting practical applicability.
Good reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameters, architecture descriptions, dataset generation protocol, and full pseudocode (Algorithm 1) are provided in the appendix.

The introduction of morphological variation into locomotion benchmarks (rather than only friction/gravity) creates a more challenging and arguably more realistic testbed than prior work, and this is documented with gait visualizations (Appendix D.2).
weaknesses: The claimed Δt → ∞ limit is operationally implemented by sampling context from an entirely different episode of the same domain, which is not strictly a temporal 'offset' but a change in trajectory identity; the information-theoretic argument (Eq. 7 discussion) is somewhat informal, and the paper does not clearly discuss potential confounds (e.g., different behavior-policy segments) introduced by this substitution.

The 'Gaussian Mixture prior' framing (Section 4.2, citing Jia et al. 2024) is imprecise: z is a continuous learned representation rather than a discrete set of mixture components, so describing peaks as discrete 'domain-specific action modalities' understates that the actual prior is a continuous family of shifted Gaussians; the connection to formal mixture-model diffusion theory is asserted rather than rigorously derived.

Baseline strength is questionable: CORRO exhibits very poor, sometimes strongly negative returns across all tasks (Table 1), which is atypical relative to reported CORRO performance in other contexts, raising concern about whether baselines were adequately tuned for the new, harder benchmark, potentially inflating the apparent margin of improvement.

Large standard deviations in several results (e.g., Walker2d, Ant OOD) are reported without significance testing, making it difficult to assess how reliably the reported average gains hold across seeds.

Only three prior baselines are compared (CORRO, Prompt-DT, Meta-DT), with the fourth ('End-to-End Diffusion') being an ablation of the authors' own pipeline; no comparison to other diffusion-based or transformer-based domain-adaptation methods beyond these is provided, limiting confidence that DADP is state-of-the-art relative to the broader literature.

The representation-quality metrics (linear probe accuracy, reconstruction loss) rely on the exact same static domain labels used to construct the Δt→∞ representations, which risks circularity in validating that this representation choice improves 'quality' rather than confirming a nearly tautological property of the construction.

The manuscript contains numerous typographical and grammatical errors (e.g., 'distangle', 'explane', 'gaussian', 'Pesudocodes', 'contructed'), suggesting insufficient proofreading, which detracts from presentation quality.

The Adroit manipulation benchmark uses only 3 domains, and it's unclear how representative or diverse these domains are for validating generalizability claims in manipulation settings; more comprehensive manipulation coverage would strengthen the claimed cross-modality generality.

No theoretical or empirical analysis of training stability for the joint noise+representation-shift prediction target (Eq. 13); potential optimization difficulties from this composite objective are not discussed.

strengths: The core intuition—that recent-context dynamics prediction entangles static domain factors with instantaneous/transient properties—is clearly motivated and illustrated with an intuitive toy example (Appendix A) and supporting t-SNE visualizations showing improved domain clustering as the context offset Δt increases.

The paper performs a fairly extensive set of ablations: effect of Δt on representation quality (linear probe accuracy, reconstruction loss), effect of representation utilization strategy (Null/Cond/w-o-Predict/w-Predict), guidance scale sensitivity, and context source flexibility (cold start vs. persistent vs. warm start), which help isolate the sources of empirical gains.

The authors extend typical locomotion benchmarks with added morphological variation to increase domain diversity, and also include a manipulation benchmark (Adroit), broadening the evaluation beyond prior narrow domain-randomization settings.
Implementation details, hyperparameters, and pseudocode (Algorithm 1) are provided in the appendix, aiding reproducibility.
The idea of injecting domain representations into the diffusion prior/target rather than purely as conditioning input is a reasonable architectural variation worth exploring.
weaknesses: There is a significant train/test mismatch in representation learning: the Δt→∞ variant pairs the context encoder with another episode entirely, yet at deployment the context is the agent's own contiguous online history (Section 5.1, Algorithm 1 evaluation). The paper does not rigorously justify why a representation trained to ignore contiguous temporal cues transfers well to inference-time contiguous rollouts beyond an informal toy-case argument; the ablation in Appendix C.2 only partially addresses this empirically without deeper analysis.

The claimed 'Gaussian Mixture' prior (Section 4.2, Figure 2) is, for any given sample/domain, simply a single Gaussian whose mean is shifted by z — effectively it is still a form of conditioning (on the mean of the noise distribution) rather than a fundamentally different mechanism from standard conditioning; the framing as 'instead of conditioning, we inject' somewhat overstates the conceptual novelty relative to simply adding a representation-dependent bias/offset term.

Several of the main-table performance gaps between DADP and the strongest baseline (Meta-DT) are not clearly separated once the reported standard deviations are considered (e.g., HalfCheetah IID 3978±66 vs. 3857±234; Ant IID 3052±30 vs. 3045±128; Ant OOD 3485±83 vs. 3187±899; Door OOD 1494±81 vs. 1294±228), undermining the paper's claim of 'consistently superior performance' across all tasks.

MetaDiffuser, explicitly identified in the related work as the closest prior method and the primary motivation for the proposed representation-learning fix, is never included as an empirical baseline in the main results (Table 1), which is a notable omission given the paper's central comparative claim against it.

The competitive 'End-to-End Diffusion' baseline (which achieves strong IID performance, e.g., comparable or even higher than some DADP variants on Walker2d) is relegated to the ablation study rather than included in the main comparison table, raising concerns about selective baseline reporting; this variant's strong performance also suggests that much of the gain may come from the diffusion backbone itself rather than the proposed representation and injection mechanisms.

The newly introduced locomotion benchmark with morphological variation is self-constructed by the authors without external validation, and all baselines are retrained/adapted internally by the authors (Appendix B.2); this raises some risk of implementation or tuning bias favoring the proposed method, particularly since no independently maintained benchmark or reproduction of baseline numbers from their original papers is used for cross-checking.

The 'mastery' metric (ratio of domains reaching 60% expert performance) is introduced without justification for the specific threshold, and no sensitivity analysis is provided to show the conclusions are robust to this choice.

The paper does not report computational overhead (training/inference time, memory) of the two-stage pipeline (encoder pretraining + diffusion policy training) relative to baselines, which is relevant given the added architectural complexity (cross-episode pairing, mixed-prior diffusion, joint denoising targets).

strengths: Clear and interesting diagnostic insight: dynamical-prediction-based domain representation learning entangles static domain factors with transient dynamical information when using temporally-adjacent context, which is illustrated convincingly with a tractable toy example (Appendix A) and validated empirically via linear-probe accuracy and reconstruction loss across different lag values (Table 2, Figure 3/6).

The proposed fix (Lagged Context Dynamical Prediction) is simple, requires no additional data generation or contrastive objectives, and is shown to transfer as a plug-in improvement to an existing method (Meta-DT, Table 3) across several additional environments, supporting generality of the idea beyond the proposed architecture.

The diffusion-injection mechanism (biasing the prior with a domain-conditioned mixed Gaussian and reformulating the denoising target) is well motivated and carefully derived (Eqs. 9–14), and the ablation in Table 4 cleanly isolates the contributions of representation quality vs. utilization strategy, showing consistent gains from each component.

Extensive ablations are provided, including sensitivity to guidance scale (Appendix C.1), robustness to different context sources at deployment (Appendix C.2), and a new 'mastery' metric that offers additional insight beyond average return.

The benchmark suite is extended beyond prior mild-randomization locomotion setups to include morphological variation and a manipulation domain (Adroit), which plausibly makes the adaptation problem harder and more realistic, and the authors commit to releasing code, datasets, and the data-generation pipeline.
weaknesses: The claim that the representation learning is fully 'unsupervised' is questionable: the training procedure (Algorithm 1) explicitly samples paired context/prediction-target pairs by rebuilding a 'domain-based paired index,' which requires knowing which episodes belong to the same domain during training. This is a form of weak/group supervision (domain/episode grouping) rather than purely unsupervised learning, and the paper does not clearly discuss this requirement or its implications for applicability when such domain groupings are unavailable.

The method's closest related work, MetaDiffuser, is discussed at length as the key baseline whose representations are claimed to be entangled, yet it is not included as an empirical baseline in Table 1; similarly, other directly relevant dynamics-prediction-based representation methods (CaDM, IIDA, CARoL) are discussed but never empirically compared against.

Scale of the empirical evaluation is modest relative to the 'extensive experiments' claim: only 4 locomotion environments (25 domains each) and 2 manipulation tasks (3 domains) are used, and the OOD domains are sampled from the same underlying parametric factor space used for training, which may represent only mild extrapolation rather than a more rigorous distribution-shift test.

Some baseline results appear unusually poor (e.g., CORRO achieving strongly negative returns in multiple environments), raising a question of whether the baseline is well-tuned/correctly adapted for the new benchmark, which could bias the perceived margin of improvement; no statistical significance testing beyond mean±std over 5 seeds is reported.

The theoretical justification for the lagged-context mechanism is limited to a simple linear toy example (ball under gravity); no analysis or guarantee is given for how well the disentanglement argument extends to the nonlinear, high-dimensional dynamics of the actual MuJoCo/Adroit environments used in the experiments.

The 'mastery' metric threshold (60% of expert performance) is introduced without justification or sensitivity analysis, and conclusions drawn from it (e.g., diffusion architectures being 'particularly well-suited' for domain adaptation) are somewhat speculative given the limited task set.
Minor presentation issues (typos such as 'guassian', 'intead', inconsistent notation between a^t and x_t in Eqs. 8–14) slightly detract from clarity and rigor.

strengths: Clear conceptual motivation: the paper identifies a concrete failure mode (entanglement of static domain factors with transient dynamical properties in context-based representation learning) and provides both an information-theoretic argument and an intuitive toy-case derivation (Appendix A, ball-projectile example) for why increasing the context offset Δt removes time-varying information while preserving static domain factors.

Extensive and largely well-designed ablations: representation-quality metrics (linear probe accuracy, reconstruction loss, within-domain std of z) across all four MuJoCo environments consistently show monotonic improvement as Δt increases toward ∞, converging near a supervised upper bound (Tables 2, 12); a separate utilization ablation (Null/Cond/w-o Predict/w Predict) isolates the benefit of biasing the diffusion prior and reformulating the target (Table 3, extended in Appendix C.7 to Hopper/Ant).

Broad empirical coverage relative to prior domain-adaptation benchmarks: four locomotion environments with added morphological variation (increasing gait diversity beyond typical friction/gravity perturbations) plus a manipulation benchmark (Adroit), evaluated under Seen/Unseen/OOD splits, which is a more demanding setup than prior CaDM/MetaDiffuser-style evaluations.

Additional robustness studies beyond the core claim (non-stationary dynamics schedules, one-step DDIM inference efficiency, alternative context sourcing strategies, guidance-scale sensitivity) that support the practical applicability of the method and show the approach is not overly brittle to hyperparameters.

Reasonably complete reproducibility materials: derivations connecting the modified forward process to a DDIM-style reverse update, full hyperparameter tables, and pseudocode for training/inference in the appendix.
weaknesses: The most directly comparable prior method (MetaDiffuser), which also injects domain representations into diffusion generation, is not empirically compared against at all; the paper only offers an indirect ablation-based argument since MetaDiffuser is 'not open-sourced.' This leaves the central claim of superiority over the closest baseline largely unverified empirically.

The Δt → ∞ strategy is implemented by 'sampling the context from another episode in the same domain,' which requires episode-level grouping by domain identity during training. While this differs from supervised parameter regression, it is a non-trivial form of weak supervision (knowing which episodes share a domain) that is not clearly discussed as a limitation relative to the 'unsupervised' framing repeated throughout the paper.

The diffusion-injection mechanism (biasing the prior with a domain-conditioned Gaussian mixture and reformulating the denoising target) is explicitly adapted from an existing structured-diffusion framework (Mixed DDIM, Jia et al. 2024); the technical novelty of this component is therefore incremental, mainly consisting of substituting domain representations for the mixture component.

Baseline strength is uneven: CORRO performs near or below zero across almost all settings (including negative scores), which is a very large gap from Meta-DT/DADP and raises questions about whether CORRO was adequately tuned/adapted for this harder benchmark, potentially inflating the apparent advantage of DADP in aggregate figures (e.g., Figure 1).

In several individual comparisons, Meta-DT remains highly competitive or statistically overlapping with DADP (e.g., Ant Unseen, Relocate Unseen, Door Seen), so the claim of 'consistently superior performance... in nearly all cases' is somewhat stronger than the per-cell numbers in Table 1 support, particularly outside the OOD setting.

The Hopper environment, lacking morphological variation, yields notably weaker representation quality (26.4% probe accuracy vs >99% supervised) even at Δt→∞, suggesting the disentanglement mechanism's benefits may be sensitive to whether domains are behaviorally distinguishable in the dataset — a limitation not fully explored beyond a post-hoc explanation.

Presentation has numerous typos and grammatical issues throughout (e.g., 'polices', 'adapation', 'guassian', 'contructed', 'distangle', 'pesudocodes') that detract from readability and suggest the manuscript would benefit from a more careful proofreading pass.

strengths: The core diagnosis—that dynamical-prediction-based representations entangle static domain factors with transient dynamical variables when using temporally-local context—is a clear, well-motivated observation, supported by an intuitive information-theoretic argument and an illustrative toy-case derivation (Appendix A).

The proposed lagged-context mechanism is simple and the paper backs it with a reasonably thorough empirical study: monotonic improvement in linear-probe accuracy, reconstruction loss, and within-domain representation variance as Δt increases (Tables 2, 12), plus t-SNE visualizations showing progressively tighter domain clustering.

Extensive ablations are provided (utilization variants, guidance scale sensitivity, context-source robustness, non-stationary dynamics, one-step DDIM inference, and a Meta-DT-based Δt ablation), which is commendable breadth for a workshop-style validation of the mechanism.

The diffusion reformulation (biasing the prior with the domain representation and folding it into the prediction target) is clearly derived algebraically and yields a plausible mechanistic story (Figure 2) for why it should help policy performance and inference-step robustness.
weaknesses: The ∆t → ∞ construction requires sampling context from 'another episode in the same domain,' which presupposes access to domain identity labels during training/data organization. This contradicts the paper's central 'unsupervised disentanglement' framing—domain grouping is itself a form of supervision, even if the specific parameter values are never used as a target. This point is not discussed as a limitation anywhere in the paper.

The comparison to the most directly relevant prior work, MetaDiffuser, is entirely indirect ('not open-sourced, so we compare implicitly via ablations'); given that MetaDiffuser is explicitly identified as the closest related method, the absence of any reimplementation or empirical head-to-head substantially weakens the paper's central claim of superiority over prior representation-injection approaches.

All quantitative baselines (CORRO 2022, Prompt-DT 2022, Meta-DT 2024) predate more recent domain-adaptive/diffusion-based approaches cited in the related work (e.g., Locoformer, In-context Q-Learning, X-Diffusion, xTED); none of these are used as empirical baselines despite being discussed, leaving the significance of the reported gains uncertain against the current state of the art.

The CORRO baseline performs extremely poorly and often achieves negative normalized returns across multiple locomotion tasks (Table 1), which is inconsistent with its reported competence in the original paper; this raises concerns about whether the baseline was properly tuned/adapted for this benchmark, and if not, the comparison is not fully fair.

The benchmark itself (MuJoCo tasks with newly introduced morphological variations) is a custom construction by the authors rather than an established or previously validated benchmark, making it hard to assess whether the reported gains would transfer to widely used domain-adaptation evaluation protocols.

The diffusion-injection technique (mixed-Gaussian prior via Mixed DDIM) is adapted fairly directly from existing structured-diffusion literature (Jia et al., 2024); the technical novelty of Section 4.2 is therefore incremental engineering rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Several reported margins between DADP and Meta-DT are within or close to overlapping standard deviations (e.g., HalfCheetah Seen: 3978±66 vs. 3857±234), and no statistical significance testing is reported, making some 'consistently superior' claims in the abstract and conclusion overstated relative to the evidence.

The claim of an 'open-sourced dataset and pipeline' is stated as a contribution but no code/dataset link is provided in the manuscript itself (only a generic 'website' for visualizations), limiting verifiability of reproducibility claims at submission time.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated diagnosis of a real problem: dynamics-prediction-based domain representations entangle static domain factors with instantaneous/transient dynamical cues when using temporally-local context, which can degrade downstream domain-conditioned policies.

The proposed fix (Lagged Context Dynamical Prediction with Δt→∞, i.e., sampling context from a different episode of the same domain) is simple, essentially hyperparameter-free, and is supported by an information-theoretic argument as well as an intuitive toy-case derivation (Appendix A) showing exactly why increasing the temporal offset removes velocity-like transient terms from the optimal representation.

The representation-injection mechanism (biasing the diffusion prior toward a domain-conditioned Gaussian mixture and reformulating the noise-prediction target to include the representation shift) is derived cleanly via DDIM algebra and is a reasonable, non-trivial way to use domain information beyond naive input-conditioning.

Extensive empirical validation: four MuJoCo locomotion environments with added morphological variation plus an Adroit manipulation benchmark, Seen/Unseen/OOD splits, multiple representation-quality metrics (linear probe accuracy, reconstruction loss, within-domain representation std), and several ablations (Δt sweep, utilization variants, guidance scale, context source, non-stationary dynamics, one-step inference efficiency, and a 'mastery' metric) that consistently corroborate the two main claims.
Good reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, dataset generation procedure and parameter ranges, baseline adaptation details, and full pseudocode are provided in the appendix.
Honest and specific limitations section acknowledging the method's restriction to stationary dynamics and outlining concrete future work.
weaknesses: No direct empirical comparison against MetaDiffuser, explicitly identified as the closest prior work; the paper only offers an indirect/ablation-based argument (via the Δt and utilization ablations) rather than a head-to-head result, which weakens the significance claim of 'superior performance over prior methods' relative to the most relevant baseline.

The chosen baselines (CORRO, Prompt-DT, Meta-DT) perform quite poorly in absolute terms in several environments (e.g., CORRO is often negative or near-zero, Prompt-DT is far below Meta-DT), raising the possibility that gains are partly attributable to weak/under-tuned baselines rather than solely to the proposed mechanisms; a comparison to a stronger diffusion-based domain-conditioning baseline beyond the paper's own 'Cond.' ablation variant would strengthen the significance case.

The 'unsupervised' framing of Δt→∞ implicitly relies on knowing which episodes belong to the same domain (used to sample the lagged context from a different episode of the same domain), which is a form of dataset-structure supervision; this should be discussed more explicitly rather than framed simply as unsupervised representation learning, since it is not purely derivable from raw unlabeled transitions without domain groupings in the training set.

The novelty of the generative-injection component is incremental relative to existing structured/mixture-prior diffusion formulations (e.g., 'Mixed DDIM' cited in the paper); the main new element is applying this to domain representations and adding the joint noise+representation prediction target, which, while useful, is a relatively modest technical step.

Task diversity is somewhat narrow: all domains share identical (S, A, R) and only transition dynamics vary, and only two locomotion environments (Walker2d, HalfCheetah) receive the deepest ablation analysis; conclusions about Ant and Hopper rely on abbreviated appendix tables, limiting the breadth of evidence for full generality.

The paper does not report compute cost or wall-clock training time comparisons across baselines, which would help contextualize the added complexity of the two-stage training pipeline (context encoder pretraining + diffusion policy training) relative to simpler end-to-end baselines.
